item.content:encoded: The person writing the manifest for the item should not be influenced by the object itself. Researchers are not supposed to access the items directly; the writing guidelines (which are not set in stone, but I feel is necessary for a properly written article) state that a researcher is supposed to instruct others on what to do during testing. And to me, it makes more sense that the write-up should be handled by someone else who is reviewing the research notes rather than someone who has been in direct contact. Because of this, the writing style comes off as antiquated to me and needs an update.

item.content:encoded:
The writing style does not mimic the effects of 714, though. 714 doesn't make you somewhat tired, it physically drains you to the point of complete fatigue; additionally, the reduced mental capacity that is brought on by 714 causes people to be unable to answer trivial questions, let alone write an entire, comprehensible document. The notes, perhaps, but it is not suggested that the author of the notes was under the influence of 714, especially considering its immediate, extreme effects on the body.

Though you may have interpreted the article as having an intentionally lackluster clinical tone, I personally believe that it wasn't intentional. Besides, it's a Series I article: standards were different and clinical tone was not as developed as it is now.

item.content:encoded:
Interesting. I was gonna say, "I don't get it, why is this scary/horrible?" Then I started reading the comments and realized this was an older skip from back when everything was still novel. Carry on! ^^

If you're seriously interested in a rewrite… start by asking yourself why the ring puts people to sleep. Who made it? Why did they make it? Is it functioning as-designed or has it gone wrong somehow? If the latter, why? What was it meant to do and why is it doing this other thing instead?

You don't need to put all of this into the skip, but you should privately know the answers before you begin reverse-engineering what the Foundation may or may not have learned about it.

The secret truth only you know should ideally be something horrible or baffling or even just incredible. Then you can hint at it all throughout the skip, leading the reader's imagination towards it but not quite saying it. Since the Foundation can't prove anything, and they're above rampant speculation. But we're not. And if you tell it right, we'll either figure out what you're hinting at… or else our imaginations will lead us somewhere even more horrible than what you'd planned.

Good luck! :D

Way overdue, but I think I've helped clear a few things up. I think the way it works now better explains the memetic protection effects; it sort of… reduces the speed at which your brain processes all information? Something like that. Most "instant-effect" memetics are processed so slowly that the meme isn't completely parsed and "executed" by the time the wearer has looked away, so nothing happens. Any memes that 'embed' themselves for later activation can still slip past it though.

A quick browse of the "Understanding Memetics" guide was quite helpful in this regard. I think.
